source_text: Αὐτίκα γοῦν τῶν τῇδε βασιλέων αἱ εἰκόνες, κἂν μὴ ἀπὸ τῆς πολὺ τιμιωτέρας ὕλης, χρυσοῦ, ἀργύρου, ἠλέκτρου ἢ ἐλέγαντος, ὦσι κατεσκευασμέναι, τιμὴν ἔχουσι πρὸς ἁπάντων· οὐ γὰρ τὰς μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς πολὺ τιμιωτέρας ὕλης τεχνημένας θεραπεύοντες ἐξολιγωροῦσι τῶν ἄλλων οἱ ἄνθρωποι, ἀλλὰ πάσας ἐπίσης τιμῶσιν, εἰ καὶ ἀπὸ γύψου ἢ χαλκοῦ ὑπάρχουσιν, καὶ ὁ δυσφημήσας εἰς ὁποτέραν οὔτε 15 ὡς πηλὸν ἀτιμάσας ἀφιεται, οὔτε ὡς χρυσὸν ἐξευτελίσας κρίνεται, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀσεβήσας τὸν βασιλέα καὶ κύριον. τὰς μὲν ἀπὸ χρυσοῦ κατεσκευασμένας εἰκόνας τοὺς αὐτοῦ ἀγγέλους, τὰς τε ἀρχὰς καὶ τὰς ἐξουσίας, »εἰς τιμὴν« καὶ δόξαν αὐτοῦ ποι<ηθέντας νο>οῦμεν νόει γὰρ μοι τὸν θεὸν τὰς μὲν ὡς ἀπὸ χρυσοῦ κατεσκευασμένας ἔχειν εἰκόνας ἑαυτοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς πνευματικῆς καθαρωτέρας οὐσίας, οἷον τοὺς ἀγγέλους, . . <καθὼς ὁ Δαυὶδ »ὁ ποιῶν«, φησίν, »τοὺς ἀγγέλους αὐτοῦ πνεύματα καὶ τοὺς λειτουργοὺς αὐτοῦ πῦρ φλέγον«<. τὰς δέ ὥσπερ ἀπὸ γύψου ἢ χαλκοῦ, οἷον ἡμᾶς· <ἔλαβε, γὰρ φησι, »χοῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς« »ὁ θεὸς» «καὶ ἔπλασε τὸν ἄνθρωπον«· τῷ γηΐνῳ γὰρ τὴν ψυχὴν ἤνωσε τὴν »κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ« γεγενημένην. ὡς οὖν πάσας ἐνταῦθα τοῦ βασιλέως τὰς εἰκόνας τιμᾶσθαι χρή . . διὰ τὴν ἐν αὐταῖς μορφήν, οὕτω δὴ καὶ ἡμᾶς <θεοῦ εἰκόνας ὑπάρχοντας — »ὁ θεὸς γὰρ ἔκτισε τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπ᾿ ἀφθαρσίᾳ καὶ εἰκόνα τῆς ἰδίας ἀιδιότητος ἐποίησεν αὐτόν«< —, ἀνένδεκτόν ἐστι θεοῦ εἰκόνας ὑπάρχοντας πρὸς ἀπώλειαν ὡς ἠτιμωμένους χωρῆσαι παντελῆ. ὅθεν καὶ κατῆλθεν εἰς τὴν καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς οἰκουμένην ὁ λόγος καὶ ἐσαρκώθη ἐκ τοῦ σώματος ὑπὸ <πολλοῦ> χρόνου διαλελυμένην, ἀναστήσῃ ἀνώλεθρον.
pass_a_gloss: For the images of the kings here, even if they are not made from very precious material, gold, silver, electrum, or ivory, have honor from all; for people honoring those made from very precious material do not despise the others, but they honor all equally, even if they exist from plaster or bronze, and the one who speaks evil against any of them is not let off as if he dishonored clay, nor is he judged as if he despised gold, but as if he acted impiously against the king and lord himself. We think that the images made from gold, his angels, the rulers and the authorities, were made for his honor and glory; for I think that God has images of himself made from spiritual and purer substance, such as the angels, just as David says, 'he who makes his angels spirits and his servants a burning fire.' And the ones made as if from plaster or bronze, such as us; for it is said, 'God took dust from the earth and formed man'; for he joined the earthly soul with the one that was made 'according to the image of God.' So, just as all the king's images are honored here because of the form in them, in the same way we, being images of God - 'for God created man for incorruption and made him an image of his own eternity' - it is not possible for images of God to be destroyed as if dishonored. Therefore, the Word came down into our world and was incarnate from the body that had been dissolved over a long time, to raise it up incorruptibly.

choices.english: according to the image of God

bible_refs.note: he who makes his angels spirits and his servants a burning fire

pass_b_english: Even the portraits of our earthly kings command universal respect, regardless of whether they are fashioned from gold, silver, electrum, or ivory, or from humbler substances like plaster or bronze. People do not venerate the costly images while despising the cheap ones; they honor every likeness equally. If anyone insults any one of these portraits, he is not excused as though he had merely slighted clay, nor is he judged as though he had merely scorned gold. Instead, he is condemned for acting impiously against the king and lord himself.

We understand the golden images to represent God's own angels—the rulers and authorities—created for his honor and glory. For it seems right to me that God possesses images of himself fashioned from a purer, spiritual substance, namely the angels, just as David says, ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his servants a burning fire’ (Psalm 104:4). The images made as if from plaster or bronze represent us. Scripture says, ‘God took dust from the earth and formed the man,’ joining the earthly soul to the one made ‘according to the image of God.’

Therefore, just as every royal portrait here is honored because of the sovereign's form it bears, so too must we—who exist as images of God—be treated with inviolable dignity. Scripture affirms, ‘God created man for incorruption, and made him an image of his own eternity.’ It is utterly impossible for God's images to be handed over to total destruction as if they were dishonored. That is why the Word descended into our world and became incarnate, taking on a body that had long been dissolving, in order to raise it up incorruptible.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text, including the distinction between the 'golden' images (angels) and 'plaster/bronze' images (humans). Pass B correctly identifies and adds the scripture citation (Psalm 104:4) for the Davidic quote, which is required by the instructions for added identifications. The translation of 'ἐπ᾿ ἀφθαρσίᾳ' as 'for incorruption' and 'κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ' as 'according to the image of God' is faithful to the prepositional sense.
